explanations.answer: Takes his relatives and chases him
explanations.explanation: That's it. Laban, Jacob's father-in-law, doesn't wait around. He takes his relatives with him and pursues Jacob (Genesis 31:23). Nobody grabs the whole family for a quick errand, so I think he means business.

explanations.answer: Sends his sons with a message
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have Laban sending anybody with a note. He goes himself, and he brings his relatives along (Genesis 31:23). Laban, Jacob's father-in-law, chose the long way, and I mean LONG.

explanations.answer: Lets him go and stays home
explanations.explanation: Laban doesn't put his feet up. He takes his relatives and pursues Jacob (Genesis 31:23). Staying home would have saved him a lot of dust, but that's not the story.
It sounds like a loophole, doesn't it? But God shuts both doors. He tells Laban, “Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad.” (Genesis 31:24). Nice words are off the table too.

Right, there's no loophole. God tells Laban, “Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad.” (Genesis 31:24). Good and bad are both covered. Laban walks into that camp with his hands tied, and I think he knows it.

Laban says he would have sent Jacob away “…with joy and singing, with tambourines and harps.” (Genesis 31:27). That's quite a send-off for somebody he's chasing across the hills now. Whatever he feels, that's the picture he paints.

explanations.answer: With a guard of his men
explanations.explanation: No guard in his offer, friend. Laban talks about music: “…with joy and singing, with tambourines and harps.” (Genesis 31:27). Picture a send-off with tambourines and harps. That's a parade, not a security detail.
No flocks come up in his offer. What Laban says is that he would have sent Jacob away “…with joy and singing, with tambourines and harps.” (Genesis 31:27). His list is all about music.

Laban says the opposite, baker. He tells Jacob, “I have power to do you great harm…” (Genesis 31:29). Then he says the God of Jacob's father spoke to him last night and told him, “Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad.” (Genesis 31:29). So Laban claims the power right to Jacob's face, and he tells him about the warning too.
Right. Laban says, “I have power to do you great harm…” (Genesis 31:29). Then he adds that the God of Jacob's father spoke to him last night. He has the power and he still doesn't use it.

Laban asks, “But why have you stolen my gods?” (Genesis 31:30). First he names Jacob's longing for his father's house, then he goes straight for the accusation. Keep your eye on those gods, because they're about to matter a lot.
Rams do show up in this passage, but not here. Laban asks, “But why have you stolen my gods?” (Genesis 31:30). The rams come later, and from Jacob's mouth.

Silver, baker? No coin gets mentioned anywhere in this moment. Laban asks, “But why have you stolen my gods?” (Genesis 31:30). He's chased Jacob for seven days (Genesis 31:23), and that's the question he finally asks. I've lost plenty of things in a junk drawer, but I never went seven days after any of them.

Jacob says it straight: “If you find your gods with anyone here, he shall not live!” (Genesis 31:32). That's a heavy thing to say, and the next line explains why it matters: Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen the idols. He promised that without knowing who had them.

No payment plan here. Jacob says, “If you find your gods with anyone here, he shall not live!” (Genesis 31:32). It's a heavy promise, and the very next line tells us Jacob didn't know who had taken them.

explanations.answer: That person will be sent away
explanations.explanation: Jacob goes further than that. He says, “If you find your gods with anyone here, he shall not live!” (Genesis 31:32). Being sent away would be the easy version. The text then tells us Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen the idols.

The text says the opposite. Right after Jacob's promise we read, “For Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen the idols.” (Genesis 31:32). Rachel is Jacob's wife and Laban's daughter. Jacob made that promise without knowing she had them.

Right. The text tells us, “For Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen the idols.” (Genesis 31:32). Rachel is Jacob's wife and Laban's daughter. So Jacob is speaking boldly with the one fact he's missing.

Laban goes through Jacob's tent, Leah's tent and the tents of the two maidservants, and “…he found nothing.” (Genesis 31:33). That's four tents and zero idols. Then he leaves Leah's tent and walks into Rachel's (Genesis 31:33). I think that's where Rachel's heart starts pounding.
Not in those tents. The text says Laban went through Jacob's tent, Leah's tent and the maidservants' tents, “…but he found nothing.” (Genesis 31:33). The idols are in the next tent, Rachel's.
No goat turns up anywhere. Laban searches Jacob's tent, Leah's tent and the tents of the two maidservants, “…but he found nothing.” (Genesis 31:33). Not one thing for him to hold up.

explanations.answer: In a saddlebag she's sitting on
explanations.explanation: Rachel “…put them in the saddlebag of her camel, and was sitting on them.” (Genesis 31:34). Hiding something right under yourself is bold. It's like stashing a cookie in your apron pocket and then standing very still.

explanations.answer: Under the floor of her tent
explanations.explanation: The text has no digging. Rachel “…put them in the saddlebag of her camel, and was sitting on them.” (Genesis 31:34). Laban searched everything in the tent and found nothing.
No grain in the story. Rachel “…put them in the saddlebag of her camel, and was sitting on them.” (Genesis 31:34). The idols are in the saddlebag, and she's sitting right there.
That's what the text says: “So Laban searched but could not find the household idols.” (Genesis 31:35). He had already looked all through the tent. After Rachel speaks, he's still empty-handed.
The text says otherwise. After Rachel speaks, we read, “So Laban searched but could not find the household idols.” (Genesis 31:35). He went through that tent and came out with nothing.

Jacob says, “Put it here before my brothers and yours, that they may judge between the two of us.” (Genesis 31:37). He asks whether Laban found anything of his. He wants both families watching, and I think that's a man who's done being quiet about it.

It's true, actually. Jacob asks, “Have you found anything that belongs to you?” Then he says, “Put it here before my brothers and yours, that they may judge between the two of us.” (Genesis 31:37). He wants the families to be the judges.
Jacob says, “…nor have I eaten the rams of your flock.” (Genesis 31:38). He's saying he looked after the flock instead of helping himself. And that's after twenty years.

Sold? Not a word about it, baker. Jacob says, “…nor have I eaten the rams of your flock.” (Genesis 31:38). He's telling Laban that after twenty years, not one ram ended up on his plate. If I'd watched a flock for twenty years, I'd want that on a plaque.
Shearing doesn't come up. Jacob says, “…nor have I eaten the rams of your flock.” (Genesis 31:38). He's listing what he didn't do with Laban's animals.

Jacob says the reverse. He tells Laban, “I did not bring you anything torn by wild beasts; I bore the loss myself.” (Genesis 31:39). So the loss landed on Jacob. Then he adds that Laban demanded payment for what was stolen by day or night.
Right. Jacob says, “I did not bring you anything torn by wild beasts; I bore the loss myself.” (Genesis 31:39). The loss was his. That's a long way from the boss taking it.
Jacob says, “…fourteen years for your two daughters…” (Genesis 31:41). Those are Rachel and Leah. Fourteen years is a long stretch of service, and Jacob counts every one of them out loud.
Blessing isn't on his list. Jacob says, “…fourteen years for your two daughters and six years for your flocks…” (Genesis 31:41). He's counting what each stretch of years was for.

A home of his own? Nice thought, but Jacob doesn't say it. He says he served “…fourteen years for your two daughters…” (Genesis 31:41). The other six years were “…for your flocks…” (Genesis 31:41). That's the full breakdown he gives Laban.

Jacob says, “If the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, had not been with me, surely by now you would have sent me away empty-handed.” (Genesis 31:42). He credits God being with him. His hands are full because of that, not because of Laban.
That's not the word he uses. Jacob says Laban would have sent him away “empty-handed.” (Genesis 31:42). He says it would have happened if the God of his father had not been with him.

No chains in this story. Jacob says, “…surely by now you would have sent me away empty-handed.” (Genesis 31:42). He points to the God of his father being with him as the reason that didn't happen. Chains would make for a much scarier speech, but empty hands is what he actually says.

Laban says, “Come now, let us make a covenant, you and I, and let it serve as a witness between you and me.” (Genesis 31:44). He goes from chasing to making an agreement. I think the dream from the night before is still on his mind.

explanations.answer: That Jacob come back with him
explanations.explanation: Nope, friend, Laban never says “come back with me.” He says, “Come now, let us make a covenant, you and I…” (Genesis 31:44). After seven days of chasing, I bet Jacob was braced for a LOT of things. A handshake was not on the list! I think I'd have checked behind me for the catch.
Laban doesn't offer a split. He says, “Come now, let us make a covenant, you and I, and let it serve as a witness between you and me.” (Genesis 31:44). That's the plan he puts on the table.

Jacob tells his relatives, “Gather some stones.” They “…took stones and made a mound…” (Genesis 31:46). Before that, Jacob had set up one stone as a pillar (Genesis 31:45). And the text says they ate there by the mound. A pile of stones and a meal right beside it, I like it.
They don't build a wall. The relatives “…took stones and made a mound…” (Genesis 31:46). A pile instead of a wall is a lot less work.

No tower here, friend. The relatives “…took stones and made a mound…” (Genesis 31:46). Jacob had also set up one stone as a pillar (Genesis 31:45). A tower means stacking stones higher and higher, and my mustache gets tired just thinking about it.
Laban declares, “This mound is a witness between you and me this day.” (Genesis 31:48). A pile of stones can't talk, but it can stay put. That's all a witness like that needs to do.
It's not a gift. Laban says, “This mound is a witness between you and me this day.” (Genesis 31:48). It's there to be seen and remembered.

Grave, baker? Close, because a mound of stones can look like one. But Laban says, “This mound is a witness between you and me this day.” (Genesis 31:48). The text calls it a witness and says nothing about a burial. Hold on to that word witness.

That's what Laban says: “If you mistreat my daughters or take other wives, although no one is with us, remember that God is a witness between you and me.” (Genesis 31:50). Nobody else may be around, but God is. That's the thing he wants Jacob to remember.

It's true, baker. Laban says, “If you mistreat my daughters or take other wives, although no one is with us, remember that God is a witness between you and me.” (Genesis 31:50). Even with no one else around, God is a witness. Laban puts that right in the agreement.
Laban says, “If you mistreat my daughters or take other wives…” (Genesis 31:50). Those are his two conditions. He ties them both to God being a witness.
Flocks aren't in this warning. Laban says, “If you mistreat my daughters or take other wives…” (Genesis 31:50). His concern here is the daughters.
Laban says nothing about Jacob coming back. His words are, “If you mistreat my daughters or take other wives…” (Genesis 31:50). Those are the two things he names.

Laban says it goes both ways. He says, “…I will not go past this mound to harm you, and you will not go past this mound and pillar to harm me.” (Genesis 31:52). Both men promise not to pass the stones to harm the other. Jacob is no more free to harm Laban than Laban is to harm him.
Right, it's mutual. Laban says, “…I will not go past this mound to harm you, and you will not go past this mound and pillar to harm me.” (Genesis 31:52). Both men are bound by it.

explanations.answer: He swears by the Fear of Isaac
explanations.explanation: The text says, “So Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.” (Genesis 31:53). Isaac is Jacob's father. Laban talked about the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, and Jacob answered by swearing by the Fear of his own father.

explanations.answer: He refuses to swear at all
explanations.explanation: He doesn't refuse. The text says, “So Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.” (Genesis 31:53). Isaac is Jacob's father. Jacob takes the oath.
Not those. The text says, “So Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.” (Genesis 31:53). Isaac is Jacob's father. Those gods of Laban's were the topic earlier, but not here.

That's not how the text goes. After the meal, “…they spent the night on the mountain.” (Genesis 31:54). Laban gets up “Early the next morning…” and leaves then (Genesis 31:55). He didn't leave that same night.

Right, baker! After they ate, “…they spent the night on the mountain.” (Genesis 31:54). Nobody storms off in the dark. Laban got up “Early the next morning…” and then headed home (Genesis 31:55). Seven days of chasing, one meal, one night's sleep. That's a man who needed his rest, and I respect it.

That's what the text says: “Early the next morning, Laban got up and kissed his grandchildren and daughters and blessed them.” (Genesis 31:55). It's the goodbye he mentioned back in verse 28. He gets it in the end.

It happens, baker. The text says, “Early the next morning, Laban got up and kissed his grandchildren and daughters and blessed them.” (Genesis 31:55). Back in verse 28 he complained that Jacob didn't let him kiss them goodbye. Now he gets to, and then he heads home.
